## At a glance
**Guiding question:** When does a good ranking lead to the wrong action?

**For:** clinicians, nurses, doctoral researchers and reviewers who have to turn a predicted risk into a rule for
action · **Prerequisites:** @sec-b05 (the delirium cohort and its validation design); the 2 × 2 table is introduced
here and applied again in @sec-b09

**In the course:** [W3 · Diagnostics, prediction and evidence](https://cttir.github.io/clinical-data-science-in-r-course/lessons/w3-diagnostics-prediction-evidence.html)
and [W8 · Colloquium and decision](https://cttir.github.io/clinical-data-science-in-r-course/lessons/w8-colloquium-and-decision.html) ·
**Data:** synthetic (the 400 test patients of @sec-b05, read from `data/b05-delirium-cohort.csv`) ·
**Core reading time:** about 11 minutes
:::

## Case and decision {#sec-b06-case}

The orthogeriatric team from @sec-b05 has chosen the prespecified logistic regression for its pilot. Now the
standard operating procedure needs one number: from which predicted risk of postoperative delirium is a patient
offered proactive geriatric co-management? The ward manager remembers a slide that said “AUC 0.77” and asks whether
that settles it. The orthogeriatrician worries about something else: the oldest patients seem to be flagged almost
always, while a 74-year-old with several risk factors was not flagged last month and developed delirium. The team has
to fix a threshold, say how many alarms per week it will produce, and explain to the nursing staff which patients
will be missed. A threshold that is too low exhausts geriatric capacity; one that is too high leaves preventable
delirium unaddressed — and the two errors do not fall on the same patients.

## Core reading {#sec-b06-core}

::: {.callout-important appearance="simple" icon=false}
**Core reading** · required for W3 · about 11 minutes · ends before ‘Lab’
:::

```{r}
#| label: b06-core-compute
#| include: false
#| ref.label: [b06-read, b06-model, b06-two-by-two, b06-calibration, b06-groups]
```

A prediction model produces two kinds of information. It *ranks* patients from lower to higher risk, and it attaches
a *number* to each patient, the predicted probability. Different measures judge different parts of this output, and a
model can be good at one and poor at the other.

**Discrimination: does the ranking work?** The area under the ROC curve (AUC, also called the c-statistic) is the
probability that a randomly chosen patient who develops delirium receives a higher predicted risk than a randomly
chosen patient who does not. For our model on the `r nrow(test)` test patients it is
`r sprintf("%.2f", auc_test)`. The AUC uses only the order of the predictions; multiplying every risk by two would not
change it ([Methods in R: ROC and AUC for Logistic Models](https://cttir.github.io/methods-in-r/sec-ch-07-regression.html#sec-chapters-07-regression-roc-auc-for-logistic)).
It therefore cannot tell whether a predicted risk of 20% means that about one in five such patients develops
delirium, and it does not involve any threshold.

**Accuracy at a threshold: what happens to people?** Once the team decides to act on predicted risks of 20% or more,
every test patient falls into one cell of a 2 × 2 table (@tbl-b06-two-by-two). The table is the most direct
translation of a model into consequences, and it is clearer in absolute numbers than in percentages
[@hoffrage1998frequencies]. Of 1,000 patients like these, about `r per1000(sum(y))` will develop delirium. At the
20% threshold the model flags about `r per1000(tab["tp"]) + per1000(tab["fp"])`. Of the flagged patients, about
`r per1000(tab["tp"])` will develop delirium and about `r per1000(tab["fp"])` will not. About
`r per1000(tab["fn"])` patients who will develop delirium are not flagged. Sensitivity is
`r cdsr_percent(sens)`, the positive predictive value `r cdsr_percent(ppv)`.

| At a threshold of 20% | Delirium develops | No delirium | Total |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| Flagged (risk ≥ 20%) | `r tab["tp"]` | `r tab["fp"]` | `r tab["tp"] + tab["fp"]` |
| Not flagged | `r tab["fn"]` | `r tab["tn"]` | `r tab["fn"] + tab["tn"]` |
| Total | `r sum(y)` | `r sum(1 - y)` | `r length(y)` |

: The model of @sec-b05 at a threshold of 20% on the same 400 test patients. Unit: patient; counts are *synthetic*. {#tbl-b06-two-by-two}

**Calibration: can the number be taken at face value?** A model is calibrated when, among patients with a predicted
risk of about 20%, about 20% develop the outcome. @fig-b06-calibration groups the test patients into ten groups of
40 by predicted risk and compares the mean prediction with the observed proportion. Points near the diagonal mean
that the numbers can be read as risks. Two summaries go with the plot. The *calibration intercept* (here
`r sprintf("%.2f", cal_int)`) shows whether risks are too high or too low on average; zero is ideal. The *calibration
slope* (here `r sprintf("%.2f", cal_slope)`) shows whether they are too extreme or too timid; one is ideal
[@vancalster2019calibration]. Our model is close to the ideal on average, with a slope slightly below 1 — a mild sign
of overfitting that the counter-check in @sec-b05 made more visible.

```{r}
#| label: fig-b06-calibration
#| echo: false
#| fig-cap: "Calibration of the logistic regression on 400 synthetic test patients (103 with delirium). Points: observed proportion with delirium in ten groups of 40 patients ordered by predicted risk; vertical bars: exact binomial 95% intervals; dashed line: perfect calibration. Unit: patient; data status: synthetic."
#| fig-alt: !expr 'sprintf("Calibration plot with mean predicted risk on the horizontal axis and observed proportion with delirium on the vertical axis, both from 0 to 1. Ten points with vertical 95%% intervals scatter around the dashed diagonal. The lowest group has a mean predicted risk of %.0f%% and an observed proportion of %.0f%%; the highest group has a mean predicted risk of %.0f%% and an observed proportion of %.0f%%. %s", 100 * cal$predicted[1], 100 * cal$observed[1], 100 * cal$predicted[10], 100 * cal$observed[10], if (all(cal$lower <= cal$predicted & cal$upper >= cal$predicted)) "Every interval includes the diagonal." else "Not every interval includes the diagonal.")'
#| fig-height: 4.6
#| fig-width: 5.2
#| ref.label: b06-calibration-plot
```

**The threshold is a value judgement.** Choosing 20% means that the team accepts flagging up to four patients
without delirium (80 : 20) for each patient with delirium whom it reaches. This is not a statistical property; it
expresses how the team weighs a missed case against an unnecessary consultation. Decision curve analysis makes this
explicit by computing the *net benefit* of the model across thresholds [@vickers2006dca], and it belongs in every
evaluation of a model meant for clinical decisions [@steyerberg2010performance]. The lab computes it.

**Same model, same threshold, two groups.** @tbl-b06-groups splits the test patients by age. The model is calibrated
in both groups: the mean predicted risk is close to the observed proportion in each. Yet the consequences differ
sharply. Among patients aged 80 or older, `r cdsr_percent(grp["80+", "alarms"] / grp["80+", "n"], 0)` are flagged
and `r grp["80+", "fn"]` of `r grp["80+", "cases"]` delirium cases are missed. Among patients aged 65–79, only
`r grp["65-79", "alarms"]` of `r grp["65-79", "n"]` are flagged and `r grp["65-79", "fn"]` of
`r grp["65-79", "cases"]` delirium cases are missed. The reason is not a faulty model but the lower base rate in the
younger group, which places most of its future cases below the threshold.

| Age group | Patients | With delirium | Flagged | Cases found | Cases missed | Flagged without delirium | Mean predicted | Observed |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| 65–79 years | `r grp["65-79", "n"]` | `r grp["65-79", "cases"]` | `r grp["65-79", "alarms"]` | `r grp["65-79", "tp"]` | `r grp["65-79", "fn"]` | `r grp["65-79", "fp"]` | `r cdsr_percent(grp["65-79", "mean_pred"])` | `r cdsr_percent(grp["65-79", "observed"])` |
| 80 years or older | `r grp["80+", "n"]` | `r grp["80+", "cases"]` | `r grp["80+", "alarms"]` | `r grp["80+", "tp"]` | `r grp["80+", "fn"]` | `r grp["80+", "fp"]` | `r cdsr_percent(grp["80+", "mean_pred"])` | `r cdsr_percent(grp["80+", "observed"])` |

: Consequences of the 20% threshold in two age groups of the 400 synthetic test patients. Unit: patient. {#tbl-b06-groups}

**Four measures, four questions.** It helps to keep the measures apart by the question each answers. The AUC
answers “does the model put patients in the right order?” Calibration answers “can I read the number as a risk?” The
2 × 2 table at a threshold answers “how many patients are flagged, found and missed, and how much work follows?” Net
benefit answers “is acting on the model better than treating everybody or nobody, given how we weigh the two
errors?” A report that gives only the first answer leaves the clinical team to guess the other three. Overall
measures such as the Brier score, the mean squared difference between predicted risk and outcome, combine ranking
and calibration in one number and are useful for comparing models, but they do not replace the others
[@steyerberg2010performance] ([Methods in R: Diagnostic Test Accuracy](https://cttir.github.io/methods-in-r/sec-ch-14-clinical.html#sec-chapters-14-clinical-diagnostic-accuracy)).

**The most important assumption of this chapter is that the predicted risks are calibrated in the population and
setting where the threshold is applied.** A threshold on the probability scale is only meaningful if the probability
is right. If the outcome becomes more common, or is recorded more thoroughly, the ranking may stay as good as before
while every number is too low — and the threshold quietly stops meaning what the team decided. The counter-check
shows this.

**Question for the workshop:** The 20% threshold flags `r cdsr_percent((tab["tp"] + tab["fp"]) / length(y), 0)` of
patients, more than the 30% capacity of the team. Would you raise the threshold, accept a lower sensitivity in the
younger group, or argue for more capacity — and how would you explain your choice to a 74-year-old patient who is
not flagged?

## Lab {#sec-b06-lab}

### Step 1 · Read the teaching file and confirm the test patients

The lab reads the cohort written by @sec-b05. A checksum of the sorted test IDs proves that the test patients are the
same as there.

```{r}
#| label: b06-read
cohort <- read.csv("../data/b05-delirium-cohort.csv")
dev <- cohort[cohort$split == "development", ]
test <- cohort[cohort$split == "test", ]
stopifnot(nrow(cohort) == 1200, nrow(test) == 400, sum(test$delirium) == 103,
          length(intersect(dev$id, test$id)) == 0,
          digest::digest(sort(test$id)) == "9b43cfb98549b2a4c17e4feaca07de46")
```

### Step 2 · Refit the prespecified logistic regression

Preprocessing and model are exactly those of @sec-b05: medians from the development data, eight predictors, linear
terms.

```{r}
#| label: b06-model
core <- c("age", "cognitive_impairment", "asa", "haemoglobin", "sodium", "n_medications",
          "hours_to_surgery", "sensory_impairment")
medians <- sapply(dev[core], median, na.rm = TRUE)          # learned on development data only
impute <- function(d) { for (v in core) d[[v]][is.na(d[[v]])] <- medians[[v]]; d }
dev <- impute(dev); test <- impute(test)
fit <- glm(reformulate(core, "delirium"), family = binomial, data = dev)
p <- predict(fit, test, type = "response")                  # predicted risk, test patients
y <- test$delirium                                          # observed outcome, 0/1
auc_test <- local({ r <- rank(p); n1 <- sum(y); n0 <- length(y) - n1
  (sum(r[y == 1]) - n1 * (n1 + 1) / 2) / (n1 * n0) })
stopifnot(abs(auc_test - 0.770) < 0.001)                    # identical to B05
per1000 <- function(x) round(1000 * x / length(y))          # natural frequency per 1,000 patients
```

### Step 3 · The 2 × 2 table at a threshold of 20%

```{r}
#| label: b06-two-by-two
threshold <- 0.20
flag <- p >= threshold
tab <- c(tp = sum(flag & y == 1), fp = sum(flag & y == 0),
         fn = sum(!flag & y == 1), tn = sum(!flag & y == 0))
sens <- tab[["tp"]] / sum(y)                     # flagged among patients with delirium
spec <- tab[["tn"]] / sum(1 - y)                 # not flagged among patients without delirium
ppv <- tab[["tp"]] / sum(flag)                   # delirium among flagged patients
npv <- tab[["tn"]] / sum(!flag)                  # no delirium among non-flagged patients
stopifnot(tab[["tp"]] == 75, tab[["fp"]] == 107, tab[["fn"]] == 28, tab[["tn"]] == 190)
exact_ci <- function(x, n) binom.test(x, n)$conf.int   # Clopper-Pearson interval
round(rbind(sensitivity = c(sens, exact_ci(tab[["tp"]], sum(y))),
            specificity = c(spec, exact_ci(tab[["tn"]], sum(1 - y))),
            ppv = c(ppv, exact_ci(tab[["tp"]], sum(flag))),
            npv = c(npv, exact_ci(tab[["tn"]], sum(!flag)))), 3)
```

The intervals are wide because the denominators are small: `r sum(y)` patients with delirium for the sensitivity,
`r sum(flag)` flagged patients for the positive predictive value. Every percentage in a report should come with its
denominator ([CTTIR Courses, Course 1 · Diagnostic testing: Se, Sp, PPV, NPV, LR](https://cttir.github.io/courses/course1_foundations/labs/lab_week2_session3.html)).

### Step 4 · AUC with an uncertainty interval

Two common intervals are compared: the analytical DeLong interval [@delong1988auc] as implemented in **pROC**
[@robin2011proc], and a percentile bootstrap over patients.

```{r}
#| label: b06-auc
#| message: false
library(pROC)
roc_obj <- roc(y, p, levels = c(0, 1), direction = "<", quiet = TRUE)
ci_delong <- as.numeric(ci.auc(roc_obj, method = "delong"))[c(1, 3)]
set.seed(6062)
boot_auc <- replicate(2000, {
  i <- sample(length(y), replace = TRUE)
  as.numeric(auc(roc(y[i], p[i], levels = c(0, 1), direction = "<", quiet = TRUE)))
})
ci_boot <- quantile(boot_auc, c(0.025, 0.975))
stopifnot(abs(as.numeric(auc(roc_obj)) - auc_test) < 1e-12)
round(rbind(DeLong = ci_delong, bootstrap = ci_boot), 3)
```

Both intervals run from about `r sprintf("%.2f", ci_delong[1])` to `r sprintf("%.2f", ci_delong[2])`. With 103
events, a second model would need a clearly larger AUC before any difference could be claimed — one reason why
@sec-b05 did not crown a winner.

### Step 5 · Calibration: plot, intercept and slope

```{r}
#| label: b06-calibration
lp <- qlogis(p)                                             # linear predictor (log-odds)
cal_int <- unname(coef(glm(y ~ offset(lp), family = binomial))[1])   # calibration-in-the-large
cal_slope <- unname(coef(glm(y ~ lp, family = binomial))[2])         # calibration slope
o_e <- sum(y) / sum(p)                                      # observed / expected events
bins <- cut(rank(p, ties.method = "first"), 10, labels = FALSE)      # ten groups of 40
cal <- do.call(rbind, lapply(split(seq_along(p), bins), function(i) {
  ci <- binom.test(sum(y[i]), length(i))$conf.int
  data.frame(n = length(i), predicted = mean(p[i]), observed = mean(y[i]),
             lower = ci[1], upper = ci[2])
}))
stopifnot(all(cal$n == 40), abs(cal_int) < 0.05, cal_slope > 0.8, cal_slope < 0.95)
round(c(intercept = cal_int, slope = cal_slope, observed_expected = o_e), 3)
```

The following code draws @fig-b06-calibration in the core reading.

```{r}
#| label: b06-calibration-plot
#| eval: false
library(ggplot2)
ggplot(cal, aes(x = predicted, y = observed)) +
  geom_abline(intercept = 0, slope = 1, linetype = cdsr_linetypes[2], colour = cdsr_colours[["grey"]]) +
  geom_errorbar(aes(ymin = lower, ymax = upper), width = 0.015, colour = cdsr_colours[["blue"]]) +
  geom_point(size = 2.4, shape = cdsr_shapes[1], colour = cdsr_colours[["blue"]]) +
  coord_equal(xlim = c(0, 1), ylim = c(0, 1)) +
  labs(x = "Mean predicted risk in group", y = "Observed proportion with delirium",
       caption = "10 groups of 40 test patients; n = 400, 103 events; synthetic data") +
  theme_cdsr()
```

A smooth calibration curve is an alternative to grouped points but needs larger samples to be stable
[@vancalster2019calibration]; with 400 patients the grouped version with intervals is the more honest display
([Methods in R: Calibration Plots](https://cttir.github.io/methods-in-r/sec-ch-13-ml.html#sec-chapters-13-ml-calibration-plots)).

### Step 6 · From one threshold to many

```{r}
#| label: b06-thresholds
at_threshold <- function(t) {
  f <- p >= t
  c(threshold = t, flagged = sum(f), flagged_pct = mean(f), tp = sum(f & y == 1),
    fp = sum(f & y == 0), fn = sum(!f & y == 1), sensitivity = sum(f & y == 1) / sum(y),
    ppv = sum(f & y == 1) / sum(f), alarms_per_case = sum(f) / sum(f & y == 1))
}
thr <- as.data.frame(t(sapply(c(0.10, 0.15, 0.20, 0.30, 0.40), at_threshold)))
stopifnot(thr$flagged[thr$threshold == 0.30] <= 0.32 * length(y))   # 30% threshold fits the capacity
knitr::kable(thr, digits = c(2, 0, 2, 0, 0, 0, 2, 2, 1), row.names = FALSE,
             col.names = c("Threshold", "Flagged", "Share flagged", "Cases found", "Flagged, no delirium",
                           "Cases missed", "Sensitivity", "PPV", "Alarms per case found"),
             caption = "Consequences of five thresholds for the same model on 400 synthetic test patients (103 with delirium).")
```

The last column is the number of flagged patients per delirium case reached, the reciprocal of the positive predictive
value. Of the five thresholds, 30% is the lowest that keeps the share of flagged patients near the team's capacity of
about 30%; it does so at the price of `r thr$fn[thr$threshold == 0.30]` missed cases instead of `r thr$fn[thr$threshold == 0.20]`.

### Step 7 · Net benefit and the decision curve

Net benefit counts correctly flagged patients and subtracts flagged patients without delirium, weighted by the odds of
the threshold: NB = TP/n − FP/n × t/(1 − t) [@vickers2006dca]. It is compared with flagging everybody and flagging
nobody (net benefit 0).

```{r}
#| label: b06-dca
ts <- seq(0.05, 0.50, by = 0.01)
nb_model <- sapply(ts, function(t) { f <- p >= t
  sum(f & y == 1) / length(y) - sum(f & y == 0) / length(y) * t / (1 - t) })
prev <- mean(y)
nb_all <- prev - (1 - prev) * ts / (1 - ts)
dca <- rbind(data.frame(threshold = ts, net_benefit = nb_model, strategy = "Model"),
             data.frame(threshold = ts, net_benefit = nb_all, strategy = "Flag everybody"),
             data.frame(threshold = ts, net_benefit = 0, strategy = "Flag nobody"))
nb20 <- nb_model[which.min(abs(ts - 0.20))]
stopifnot(nb20 > nb_all[which.min(abs(ts - 0.20))], nb20 > 0)
```

```{r}
#| label: fig-b06-dca
#| fig-cap: "Decision curve for the logistic regression on 400 synthetic test patients (103 with delirium): net benefit of acting on the model compared with flagging everybody or nobody, for thresholds from 5% to 50%. Unit: patient; data status: synthetic."
#| fig-alt: "Line chart of net benefit against threshold probability from 0.05 to 0.50. The line for flagging everybody starts at about 0.22 and falls below zero at a threshold of about 0.26. The model line starts at about the same height, declines more slowly and lies on or above both alternatives across the whole range, ending at about 0.04 at a threshold of 0.50. The line for flagging nobody is constant at zero."
#| fig-height: 4
library(ggplot2)
ggplot(dca, aes(x = threshold, y = net_benefit, colour = strategy, linetype = strategy)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 0.9) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0.20, colour = cdsr_colours[["grey"]], linetype = cdsr_linetypes[4]) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c(Model = cdsr_colours[["blue"]], `Flag everybody` = cdsr_colours[["orange"]],
                                 `Flag nobody` = cdsr_colours[["grey"]])) +
  scale_linetype_manual(values = c(Model = cdsr_linetypes[1], `Flag everybody` = cdsr_linetypes[2],
                                   `Flag nobody` = cdsr_linetypes[3])) +
  coord_cartesian(ylim = c(-0.05, 0.27)) +
  labs(x = "Threshold probability", y = "Net benefit", colour = NULL, linetype = NULL,
       caption = "Vertical line: threshold of 20%. n = 400 test patients; synthetic data") +
  theme_cdsr()
```

At 20% the model's net benefit is `r sprintf("%.3f", nb20)`: the equivalent of `r round(nb20 * 1000)` correctly
flagged patients per 1,000 with no unnecessary consultations at all. Decision curves and related measures are
practised in [CTTIR Courses, Course 2 · Decision curves, NRI, IDI](https://cttir.github.io/courses/course2_regression/labs/lab_week4_session4.html).

### Step 8 · Two groups, with denominators

```{r}
#| label: b06-groups
age_group <- ifelse(test$age >= 80, "80+", "65-79")
grp <- t(sapply(c("65-79", "80+"), function(g) {
  i <- age_group == g
  c(n = sum(i), cases = sum(y[i]), alarms = sum(flag[i]), tp = sum(flag[i] & y[i] == 1),
    fn = sum(!flag[i] & y[i] == 1), fp = sum(flag[i] & y[i] == 0),
    mean_pred = mean(p[i]), observed = mean(y[i]))
}))
sens_ci <- t(sapply(rownames(grp), function(g) exact_ci(grp[g, "tp"], grp[g, "cases"])))
stopifnot(sum(grp[, "n"]) == 400, sum(grp[, "tp"]) == tab[["tp"]], sum(grp[, "fn"]) == tab[["fn"]],
          grp["65-79", "fn"] == 17, grp["80+", "fn"] == 11)
round(cbind(sensitivity = grp[, "tp"] / grp[, "cases"], lower = sens_ci[, 1], upper = sens_ci[, 2]), 2)
```

In the younger group the sensitivity is `r cdsr_percent(grp["65-79", "tp"] / grp["65-79", "cases"], 0)` with an
interval from `r cdsr_percent(sens_ci["65-79", 1], 0)` to `r cdsr_percent(sens_ci["65-79", 2], 0)`, based on only
`r grp["65-79", "cases"]` cases. The difference to the older group is large, but the younger group's estimate is
imprecise. TRIPOD+AI asks for performance estimates with confidence intervals, including for key subgroups
[@collins2024tripodai, item 23a].

## Counter-check {#sec-b06-countercheck}

**Change one assumption: how delirium is recorded.** Suppose that the ward introduces a structured delirium screen
twice a day instead of relying on notes. More mild episodes are recorded. We represent this as an *assumption*: the
log-odds of recorded delirium rise by 0.8 for every patient, while the patients and their predictors stay the same.
Because the data are synthetic, each patient's true risk is known and the new outcomes can be simulated.

*Before you run the code, predict:* Does the AUC fall, stay or rise? Does the calibration intercept move, and in which
direction? How many patients whose (new) risk is at least 20% will the unchanged 20% threshold miss?

```{r}
#| label: b06-countercheck
set.seed(6061)
risk_b <- plogis(qlogis(test$true_risk) + 0.8)              # true risk under the new recording (assumption)
y_b <- rbinom(length(risk_b), 1, risk_b)                    # recorded delirium, setting B
auc_b <- as.numeric(auc(roc(y_b, p, levels = c(0, 1), direction = "<", quiet = TRUE)))
cal_int_b <- unname(coef(glm(y_b ~ offset(lp), family = binomial))[1])
missed_high_a <- sum(test$true_risk >= threshold & !flag)   # true risk >= 20%, not flagged, setting A
missed_high_b <- sum(risk_b >= threshold & !flag)           # same, setting B
sens_b <- sum(flag & y_b == 1) / sum(y_b)

# Intercept update: estimate the shift on 200 patients, check it on the other 200
half <- seq_along(p) <= 200
shift <- unname(coef(glm(y_b[half] ~ offset(lp[half]), family = binomial))[1])
p_upd <- plogis(lp + shift)
cal_int_upd <- unname(coef(glm(y_b[!half] ~ offset(qlogis(p_upd[!half])), family = binomial))[1])
stopifnot(abs(auc_b - auc_test) < 0.05, cal_int_b > 0.5, missed_high_b > 3 * missed_high_a,
          abs(cal_int_upd) < abs(cal_int_b))
knitr::kable(data.frame(
  quantity = c("Recorded delirium", "AUC", "Calibration intercept", "Sensitivity at 20%",
               "Patients with true risk ≥ 20% not flagged"),
  setting_a = c(paste0(sum(y), "/400"), sprintf("%.2f", auc_test), sprintf("%.2f", cal_int),
                cdsr_percent(sens), paste0(missed_high_a, " of ", sum(test$true_risk >= threshold))),
  setting_b = c(paste0(sum(y_b), "/400"), sprintf("%.2f", auc_b), sprintf("%.2f", cal_int_b),
                cdsr_percent(sens_b), paste0(missed_high_b, " of ", sum(risk_b >= threshold)))),
  col.names = c("Quantity", "Setting A (as developed)", "Setting B (structured screen)"),
  caption = "Counter-check: same model, same 400 synthetic patients, outcome recorded more thoroughly (assumption: +0.8 on the log-odds scale).")
```

The ranking survives: the AUC is `r sprintf("%.2f", auc_b)` instead of `r sprintf("%.2f", auc_test)`. The numbers do
not. The calibration intercept of `r sprintf("%.2f", cal_int_b)` means that the model systematically underestimates
risk in setting B, and `r missed_high_b` patients whose risk now exceeds the 20% that the team agreed on are not
flagged — compared with `r missed_high_a` in setting A. A team that monitored only the AUC would notice nothing.
Updating the intercept on 200 patients from the new setting and checking it on the other 200 reduces the calibration
intercept to `r sprintf("%.2f", cal_int_upd)`. TRIPOD+AI asks authors to describe such model updating and to report
the updated model [@collins2024tripodai, items 12f and 24]. A different hospital with a higher baseline risk would
produce the same pattern; @sec-b19 and @sec-b20 take this further.

## Consequences for patients and operations {#sec-b06-consequences}

**Patients and fairness.** The age-group table is the core ethical finding of this chapter. With a single threshold,
patients aged 65–79 who will develop delirium are missed far more often than older patients, although the model is
calibrated in both groups. Lowering the threshold for the younger group would find more of their cases at the cost of
more consultations without delirium; it is a value decision that should be made openly, with the affected clinicians
and, where possible, patient representatives, and not hidden in code (@sec-b21;
[Strategy in R: Fairness in Machine Learning](https://cttir.github.io/strategy-in-r/sec-fairness-ml.html)). A
patient who is not flagged must still receive the usual clinical attention; the threshold allocates an additional
offer, it does not withdraw care.

**Operations.** If about eight eligible patients are admitted per week (*assumption*), the 20% threshold produces
about `r round(8 * mean(flag), 1)` alarms per week and the 30% threshold about
`r round(8 * thr$flagged_pct[thr$threshold == 0.30], 1)`. The procedure should state the threshold, the expected
alarms per week, the expected missed cases per 100 patients and the person who reviews these numbers each month.
Because calibration can drift unnoticed, monitoring must include observed versus predicted events, not only alarms
and AUC (@sec-b20).

**Regulation and documentation.** The threshold is part of how the software is used. If a manufacturer's
documentation specifies performance at a particular threshold, a local change of threshold changes the conditions
under which that claim was made; who may change it, and how this is documented, is a question for the intended
purpose and quality management (@sec-b22, *open* for the local setting).

**Data protection.** The analyses here use aggregated test results. Subgroup tables with very small cells can make
individuals identifiable when published; the rules in @sec-b26 apply before such tables leave the team.

## Look up and transfer {#sec-b06-lookup}

**Reviewer question:** “Do the authors report calibration (plot, intercept and slope) in the population where the
model is meant to be used, and do they translate their chosen threshold into absolute numbers of flagged, found and
missed patients — with denominators and intervals for key subgroups?” TRIPOD+AI asks for the measures and plots used
to evaluate discrimination, calibration and clinical utility, and for subgroup estimates with confidence intervals
[@collins2024tripodai, items 12e and 23a].

**Self-test:** A colleague reports that a delirium model “performs well” in a rehabilitation clinic: AUC 0.80. In
this clinic delirium occurs in 8% of patients, but the mean predicted risk is 24%. The clinic plans to use a 20%
threshold. What do you expect for the number of alarms and the positive predictive value, and what would you ask for
before the threshold is adopted?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Answer"}
The model overestimates risk by a factor of about three on average (calibration-in-the-large is poor), so a 20%
threshold on these inflated numbers will flag many patients whose true risk is far below 20%. Expect a high share of
flagged patients and a low positive predictive value — at an 8% base rate, most alarms will concern patients without
delirium. The AUC of 0.80 does not contradict this, because it ignores the absolute level of the predictions. Before
adoption, ask for a calibration plot with intercept and slope in this clinic, a recalibration (at least of the
intercept) on local data, and a table of flagged, found and missed patients per 100 at the proposed threshold.
:::

**Annotated sources:**

- @vancalster2019calibration explains why poor calibration can make an algorithm misleading for decisions and how to
  assess calibration at validation.
- @steyerberg2010performance sets out the framework of overall performance, discrimination, calibration and
  decision-analytic measures used in this chapter.
- @vickers2006dca introduces decision curve analysis and the link between threshold probability and the weighing of
  false-positive and false-negative decisions.
- @delong1988auc and @robin2011proc are the method and software for the analytical AUC interval in Step 4.
- @hoffrage1998frequencies shows that natural frequencies improve diagnostic reasoning compared with probabilities,
  supporting the per-1,000 translation.
- @collins2024tripodai provides the reporting items for performance measures, subgroup estimates and model updating.
